/MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Issued at 256 AM MST Fri Nov 13 2026

Guidance continues to support a fairly strong ridge developing 
Monday over the Rockies as an upper-level low exits to the 
southeast. Concurrently, an embedded shortwave should be 
departing our area to the east. Northwest flow aloft is 
anticipated as this ridge builds to the north of the County 
Warning Area (CWA). On Tuesday, NBM output is in general 
agreement with the global ensembles that the ridge becomes 
positively tilted, shifting upper- level winds to be from the 
southwest as this system propagates to the east. Furthermore, a 
longwave trough draped across the Pacific Coast lurks nearby. 
This next system is likely to weaken a bit Wednesday, ejecting 
quite a strong jet through the Central Plains in the process. 
The upper-level pattern becomes a bit more uncertain heading 
into Thursday but the majority of models suggest a weak mini- 
ridge to set up briefly over the CWA then push eastward. 
Finally, ensembles are beginning to detect another strong cutoff
low that moves onshore over the Pacific Northwest late 
Thursday. This new feature will need to be monitored through the
weekend as well.

Surface analysis projects high pressure to form with the 
ridging system and last through early Wednesday. A weak surface 
low could influence the Tri-State area later on Wednesday via 
troughing aloft. Said low should track to the northeast, keeping
potential impacts minimal. There is a cold front expected from 
this system though, which slightly boosts rainfall chances 
heading into Thursday. Furthermore, due to the positioning of 
the system off to the northwest, most of any precipitation that 
falls would be in the northern parts of our CWA and into 
southwest Nebraska. WPC currently has QPF forecasted in the 0.01
to 0.05 range so any rain would be minimal with light 
accumulation expected. Pre-frontal dewpoints in the low/mid 40s 
with relative humidities (RHs) in the 50-70% range do support 
precip. However, current Probability of Precipitation (PoP) 
guidance has us around 15-25% so confidence is low on 
accumulations for the time being.

Temperatures during this long-term forecast period are likely 
to follow a warming trend early to mid-week with high-pressure 
aloft and subsidence throughout the region. Highs in the low to 
mid 50s Monday increase to mid/upper 50s Tuesday then upper 
50s/low 60s Wednesday. A weak cold front is forecasted to drop 
high temps slightly for Thursday but some locations in the 
eastern part of the CWA may still reach the 60s. Overnight low 
temperatures should drop to around freezing Monday and Tuesday 
mornings (low/mid 30s) then rise into the 35-42 degree range 
Wednesday morning. Lows on Thursday may be variable with low 30s
possible for western areas of the CWA and low 40s for eastern 
locations. 

Surface winds should be breezy during this period, especially 
when that jet streak moves overhead on Wednesday. 15-25 mph 
sustained southerly winds Monday, strengthening to 20-30 mph 
Tuesday is likely. Winds shift to to southwest Wednesday but 
remain strong at 20-30 mph. At last, winds die down quite a bit 
to 5-15 mph. Gusting up to 40 mph is likely across the Tri-State
area through Wednesday, especially in some locations of our 
eastern Colorado counties. 45-50 mph gusts will be possible on 
Wednesday across those more wind prone areas. Despite the gusty 
winds, fire weather concerns remain minimal as relative 
humidities are actually forecasted to be much higher than even 
elevated conditions would support. RHs consistently above 40% 
are likely through midweek. Thursday should be the driest day 
across our coverage area, but again with RHs above even elevated
fire weather criteria. Values as low as 35% west of US-385 are 
possible. Widespread overnight RHs may increase to 100% Monday 
and Tuesday mornings with radiational cooling; thus, fog will be
possible next week.
